evidence: Cic. Tusc. 3.52: maris subita tempestās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday word: what comes on all at once, a storm, a death, a fright. Lewis & Short also gives it for soldiers raised in haste (Tac. H. 4.76) and, of a slope, steep (Stat.); as a noun, subitum is something that has suddenly come up, an urgent matter (subitum est ei remigrāre, Cic. Fam. 13.2). The adverb is subitō (see suddenly).

Sudden as against expected or prepared: Cicero sets it against exspectātus and against meditātus et praeparātus (Lewis & Short). Of people it means upstart (ignōtī hominēs et repentīnī, Cic. Brut. 242, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Agr. 2.60: amor tam imprōvīsus ac tam repentīnus
terms.comment: Not foreseen, the point being that no one saw it coming. Its ablative makes an adverb: dē imprōvīsō, suddenly, without warning.

phrases.english: silence falls, and a sudden calm

phrases.latin: namque ista subita mē jubet benignitās vigilāre, faciās nē meā culpā lucrum
phrases.english: for this sudden kindness of yours tells me to stay awake, so that you make no profit through my fault

phrases.latin: Unde iste amor tam imprōvīsus ac tam repentīnus?
phrases.english: Where does this love of his come from, so unforeseen and so sudden?

phrases.latin: Leviōra enim sunt ea, quae repentīnō aliquō mōtū accidunt, quam ea, quae meditāta et praeparāta īnferuntur.
phrases.english: For wrongs done on some sudden impulse are lighter than those that are thought out and prepared.
